title: About me!
body_html:
Hello COETAIL (Online 12) community. I am Luis Carlos from Venezuela. I have been living in Panama for almost 14 years now. This is my 4th year working at the International School of Panama, where I started as a Learning Support Specialist and eventually became their Educational Technology Coordinator.

Next year, my role at school will be more focused on STEM/Tech Coaching. Thus, I wanted to find a new learning experience that could help me with this new role and professional growth. I am lucky enough to have amazing colleagues such as Joel Bevans and Sarah Schnack as part of the Teaching and Learning Department at our school. They helped me out with suggestions of the best options for me, and I finally decided that COETAIL was the right choice.

In this journey, I am looking forward to being inspired by educators worldwide, learning about innovative pedagogical ideas, and forming new connections.

title: My communities
My ISTE Learning Goals
body_html:
At the school I work, the ISTE standards have been used by some of our tech integrators to guide their collaboration with teachers when planning or co-teaching. The school aims to use the ISTE framework to embed technology in our curriculum and improve the use of technology in class. This year I tried to align this school goal as one of my own goals on my Personal Learning Pathway but failed to accomplish it as many other opportunities shifted this goal down on my list of priorities. Next year, I want to retake this goal, beginning my journey with the administration. I believe all administrators should be role models and be proficient in what they expect teachers to do. I want them to be confident about the ISTE standards, what they mean, and how they can be implemented before asking the staff to jump-in in yet another initiative.

This school year, to get more familiarized with the standards and connect with colleagues with similar goals, I asked my school to send me to the ISTE Creative Constructive Lab, an interactive learning experience exposing attendees to how to create media-rich learning environments and experiences. I attended and learned a lot, met new people, got inspired. However, I was missing the more theoretical part of it. I think I am already receiving support from my school by just being part of the COETAIL community.

This being said, all standards are relevant to me, but if I need to select the ones that I believe will help my institution and me, it would be these:

1a -Set professional learning goals to explore and apply pedagogical approaches made possible by technology and reflect on their effectiveness.

2c -Model for colleagues the identification, exploration, evaluation, curation, and adoption of new digital resources and tools for learning.

4a -Dedicate planning time to collaborate with colleagues to create authentic learning experiences that leverage technology.

4c -Use collaborative tools to expand students' authentic, real-world learning experiences by engaging virtually with experts, teams, and students, locally and globally.

title: From Lurker to Connector
body_html:
When I first started reviewing the resources for ¨From Lurker to Connector¨, I immediately thought of The Tipping Point by Malcolm Gladwell. In the second chapter, “The law of the few,” Gladwell writes about people who are critical to social epidemics, whom he calls Connectors, Mavens and Salesmen, and describes them as people with a special gift for bringing the world together. After referring to the idea of six degrees of separation, closely related to connectors, Malcolm asked and answered this question:

“What makes someone a Connector? The first — and most obvious — criterion is that Connectors know lots of people. They are the kinds of people who know everyone. All of us know someone like this. But I don’t think that we spend a lot of time thinking about the importance of these kinds of people. I’m not even sure that most of us really believe that the kind of person who knows everyone really knows everyone. But they do.” 

For Malcolm, the importance of connectors goes far beyond the number of people they know; it is also about the kind of people they know:

“...they are people whom all of us can reach in only a few steps because, for one reason or another, they manage to occupy many different worlds and subcultures and niches… ...their ability to span many different worlds is a function of something intrinsic to their personality, some combination of curiosity, self-confidence, sociability, and energy.”

If I would ask my colleagues if they would describe me as Malcolm describes connectors in his book, I am sure they would (some self-confidence, right?). When I purposefully think about the different worlds I am part of: education, telecommunications, financial, gastronomy, engineering, non-profit, literature, entrepreneurial, I believe I am a good candidate to be a connector, and sometimes I am. So, what is the missing ingredient for me to be a connector?

Have you read The Circle by Dave Eggers? Spoiler alert! Spoiler alert! (Not really).

Yes, sometimes, I am a lurker. Yes, sometimes, I am a connector. But, am I both a lurker and a connector in my professional life? No. The scenarios in which both of these roles happen are different for sure. As a traveler, I like to document my trips with pictures and videos and post on social media. I stay with locals. I narrate stories about interesting facts, give my colleagues, friends, and family suggestions on what to visit, create lists of experiences, places, and restaurants and have them ready to share with anyone asking for tips. I create content. I share, I am definitely a connector.

As an educator, the story goes differently. I still create the experiences, design escape rooms, co-teach classes using a simulator, and co-plan a science/math unit with my colleagues, among other initiatives. I differentiate, modify, accommodate, create academic content, train staff, take pictures, record videos. Still, it does not go beyond that colleague I am working with, my department, my division, and - if I am lucky - my school.

Why? Because I'm scared. Because it is English and not Spanish. Yes, there are other factors, but the main reason is that I am not as confident writing and posting on social media or a blog or even commenting on another person’s post even when my desire to do it is strong. To document my trips, I choose whether to add a description in English or Spanish. In most instances, I will tend to do it in Spanish as I feel extremely confident writing in my mother tongue. I have short stories in Spanish published in books and magazines. I wrote a song in Spanish that made it onto an album. And I plan to do the same as an educator. Just writing this post, I second guess every single word I type. That is why I believe COETAIL is more than an amazing learning experience. It is also a great challenge and opportunity to embrace myself as the connector I fully am.

title: Research in the digital age
body_html:
When talking about research in the digital age, it is fair to say that there are countless tools that may make this process easier. Nowadays, the proliferation of data on the internet has made access to information only a click away. Just a few minutes sitting behind the screen and you will be exposed to infinite amounts of information, even if you are not actively seeking.

The world is currently experiencing a pandemic that will change the research process as we know it. Since the Covid-19 crisis began, society is proving that working from home --in our case, teaching from home-- is not only possible but could be even more productive and efficient than the status quo.

In education, online learning is drastically changing the learning process and shifting the mindsets of teachers and students regarding the whole learning experience. Teachers are moving away from online single tasks or assignments and instead are exposing students to a more project-based, exploratory, and asynchronous inquiry.  Through access to emails, shared documents, collaborative platforms, and video conferencing, educators have managed to work with all stakeholders in a way, perhaps less formal, but definitely no less efficient.

But it’s not all rainbows and roses when it comes to access to information and the wide variety of digital tools. Inevitably, there are some negatives in this equation.  The National Research Council (2001), in their book Issues for Science and Engineering Researchers in the Digital Age, states:

“...these new digital tools—because they are so powerful and easy to use—can be misused by the unsophisticated or abused by the dishonest. They may offer new temptations for plagiarism and fraud. Researchers may find themselves overwhelmed by the massive volume of data on the networks as they seek ways to winnow sound information from nonsense. Protecting the integrity of research will require vigilance and ingenuity and probably the development of new technologies to enhance the security of data and prevent forgeries, use of false identities, and unauthorized changes to publications or data.”

Our students face these challenges and temptations every day. Those long hours that my generation spent at the library reviewing several books to gather the information are now unpacked and available online. Today, students are flooded with data related to their search. The hard work comes when it is time to filter the data, determining its credibility and reliability to convert it into useful information. Luckily, there are several techniques and strategies to help us with the task of refining our search and maximizing the use of search engines. Google has put together a lot of resources to help users learn How to search (link), and How to use search operators (link). Below, some commonly used operators.

 

Once the filter has been narrowed down, we need to make sure to follow appropriate academic honesty principles, citing the authors according to the required style formats. There are also online tools that facilitate this task, such as:

EasyBib: Automatic works cited and bibliography formatting for MLA, APA, and Chicago/Turabian citation styles. Now supports the 7th edition of MLA.

BibMe: Free Bibliography & Citation Maker - MLA, APA, Chicago, Harvard.

Finally, educators must ensure that sources are indeed used transparently,  properly citing evidence and information. But fortunately, there is a good thing for us teachers, there are systems that have been developed to make teacher verification for authenticity much easier. Turnitin used to be basically alone in this field, but recently Google released the Google Originality Reports and although Turnitin is still king in this field, Google has entered the market with a free service that is sure to catch some eyes.

I ran Google Originality Reports for this post and here are some images showing the results.

title: The Power of Web Design
body_html: Our websites or blogs are (or can be, at least) a key part of our fairly important virtual presence. When people visit our websites, the way it looks or even little details like where on the screen the most relevant information is located, influence how the viewer perceives us as professionals. When building our websites, or when COETAIL forces us to improve them (haha), having best practices in mind will generally define our viewers' experiences. In short: good web design is important, bad web design can make your site look unprofessional and make it difficult for you to attract, engage, and earn visitors’ trust. I visited my website as a viewer and tried to find areas of improvement. As our website design right now is not entirely up to us, I tried to implement as many of the changes that were possible. However, I will also mention the ones that I would like to consider later when I have more control over my website. If there were no restrictions, one of the first things I could change is my domain’s name or URL (around $12 a year for those of you wondering). I thought of a URL like mrmorenoteach or something similar as this represents what I want to achieve with my website more accurately. Godday.com is a very popular domain seller and host provider, and they offer a free domain with their web hosting services. Theme. In my case, the button with this option is missing because it is a multisite install. The Add New button only appears when you go to the top bar -> My Sites -> Network Admin -> Themes. From there, you can add new themes and enable them for the rest of the network. We have some options, but there are plenty of enhanced themes that would allow us to have innovative-looking websites in an easier way. Besides the web design itself, there is a lot involved in actual post creation. You will notice that I have been trying to include more images to make posts less text-heavy and more visually appealing. At the end of the day, who has the time to read 13,700 words of content? A simple thing that I changed was my Permalink Settings. First I had Day and name and changed to Post name.   Before: [image: image34-300x25.jpg] [image: image13-300x142.jpg] After:  [image: image5-300x26.jpg] [image: image35-300x146.png] This looks much better and makes our website URLs super clean.  Then I decided to change my website title, tagline, and site icon.   Before Title: LUIS' COETAIL JOURNEY Tagline: Not just another COETAIL site Site icon: Default [image: image25-300x88.png] [image: image9-300x42.png] [image: image40.png] After Title: Mr. Moreno Teach Tagline: Bringing the world into my classroom Site icon: My Bitmoji  [image: image36-300x88.png] [image: image20-300x54.png] [image: image19-300x300.png] [image: image7.png] Logo. For now, I decide to use my Bitmoji as my logo as I had it created already and I don’t have the time to think about the perfect logo right now (that’s a whole separate project!). Besides that, many teachers around the globe have chosen to use Bitmoji and create virtual classrooms to build community (among other reasons) during distance learning. And the kids are loving it! Before: None. [image: image28-300x57.png] After: [image: image16-233x300.png] [image: image41-300x60.png] Menu. After a long exploration of my site, I realized I didn’t have menus enabled. Before: [image: image6-1-300x135.png] After: [image: image31-1-238x300.png] [image: image38-1-300x204.png] [image: image12-1-300x78.png] Adding a contact form. Yes, we have the comment options but there is no way for our visitors to contact us privately. I already added the option in the menu bar, but I will create the actual Contact Form later. At the end of the day we want to build connections, don’t we?   What other suggestions do you have?

title: The Number Talk
body_html:
I believe good infographics, ideally, don't require a lot of explanation. Good infographics present information in an engaging pre-digested way. Here is the infographic I have been working on to show the demographic data related to students and staff at the school I work at, the International School of Panama. [image: Copia-de-COETAIL-Infographics-3.png] After long hours of work to finish this product, here are some of my reflections.
  • Renweb (FACTS) or any Student Information System (SIS) your school uses is a great starting point to create infographics about your school.
  • Creating a Renweb report is fairly easy when the data is complete and updated.
  • ISP needs to update and standardize the information in our SIS.
    • There are students and staff that have already left and are still active in Renweb.
    • There is a lot of missing information that I consider important to be culturally sensitive, inclusive, and even cautious (such as medical conditions). I understand that the medical staff manages allergies and all other medical or alimentary restriction information, but this information is relevant for other purposes and, efficiency-wise, should all be consolidated under one system.
      • Allergies: When going on field trips, we could get the information needed from here instead of requesting it from the medical staff.
      • Dietary restrictions: We could analyze dietary restrictions to create different menus at our school, for example. Being a vegetarian, I always feel left out and with few options.
      • Religion: I really wanted to know about other culturally important facts like the religions followed by our staff and students, but we don’t have this information.
      • Ethnicity: We claimed to be an inclusive and diverse school, but there is no accurate data about ethnicity or race, to mention a couple.
      • Type of hire: Local or foreign contracts.
  • Good infographics take time to put together. Pulling the data takes little time. Analyzing the data requires certain skills, like understanding spreadsheets, formulas, and more.
  • Stick to a color palette and typography. Consistency is key when designing infographics.
  • Use a template. A great way to help you out and guarantee a great outcome is to use a design tool like Canva or a template like slidesgo (I used this one) or slidescarnival.
  • You can put together infographics using only Google Slides. I did.
  • Pick the right type of graph to represent your data. I had to either change the graph after realizing it wasn't the best choice or keep only the most relevant information or the ones with the biggest percentages. For example, I started with this:
[image: COETAIL-Infographics-4.png] And changed to this: [image: languages.png]
  • This is the first time I have created an infographic, and it helped me understand the importance of presenting data more effectively. It also made me reflect on all the data I was working with. It is a great process, but it is time-consuming. I will only consider creating an infographic if I can take advantage of it to support decision-making processes or create awareness of important topics.
Now, let the numbers talk!

title: Design rules are meant to be broken
body_html:
I love good design. There’s nothing like a well-thought-out and alluring presentation—choosing the right colors, object distribution, font size, and amount of information. There are many rules out there about PowerPoint presentations that I have heard since I was in middle school, and before Google Slide even existed. Therefore these rules were created with PowerPoint in mind but can apply to any platform or tool, online or not.
    • The 10/20/30 Rule of PowerPoint presentations: 10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point font size.
    • The 5/5/5 rule: No more than five words per line of text, a maximum of five lines of text per slide, and no more than five text-heavy slides in a row.
    • The 6x6 Presentation Rule: include no more than six words per line and no more than six bullet points per slide.
    • Rule of 7x7 in PowerPoint: (see above +1)
You get the idea; there are more rules than features in PowerPoint, and when you have learned these rules, you should be able to count by tens and know all the multiplication tables. Jokes aside, as a student, these rules were helpful to keep me focused on relevant information, to guarantee that I knew the topic/content that I was going to present, and to save my teachers and peers from the horrible torture of sitting there reading text from the slides in unison. The thing is, these rules do not always apply. They should work as a reference to help you present your points in the best way possible. It’s more about balance than anything else. Consider, for example, incorporating an 8-word quote. It would be best if you didn’t try to find one with seven words, post it incomplete in your presentation, or leave the last word on another line by itself not to break the rules. It is about balance. Now, Google Slides are more than just presentations. Commonly, we share the presentation with the audience not only as a reference but to interact with it or that the purpose of the slide is not to present something: Hyperlinks slides, digital journals, videos, activities, collaboration spaces, agendas, asynchronous lessons, online classroom with bitmojis, manipulatives, graphic organizers, infographics to mention a few. Google Slide itself is a powerful design tool, and we should also consider best practices when it comes to using it to create powerful, engaging, and efficient visual content. Let's start with an example from COETAIL itself. Our cohort page. I like the design with our pictures and names: [image: coetail-team.png] And then we have this table with links to our Twitter profiles and COETAIL blogs: [image: Cohort-blogs.png] I started by modifying our table a little bit by adding some colors and formatting it: [image: Presentación-sin-título.png] Then I realized it wasn’t enough and that to make it more efficient, both our pictures and names poster should be put together with our Twitter profile and COETAIL blog links. I decided I wanted to use the COETAIL color palette to keep it consistent. This is the result. [image: coetail-infografics-team-1.png] Our pictures can be used instead of the avatars, and we can easily find who we are looking for. To put this together, I used a Team Infographic Template from slidesgo, and all of this was designed using Google Slides. Another COETAIL example. This overview you can download as a PDF or access directly on the website: [image: overview-coetail.png] I used Canva to make the information more digestible. The information is the same but follows a vertical timeline structure making the reading process more manageable. I used the same COETAIL color palette and kept it simple with only one or two typographies. Here is the result. [image: COETAIL-Overview.png] At our school this year, instead of setting a Google Classroom for our Professional Learning Pathway process as we the two previous years, we decided to create a Slide Deck for each staff member to have all the information consolidated in one place, but also to keep track of the self-assessment, reflections, inquiry questions, and event meetings with the admin. I wanted the slides to look professional and easily understood and digested by staff, so I tried to redesign the slides. I will only show some examples as this slide deck had many slides.    Here is the before of the timeline for the process: [image: plp-original.png] Again, I considered just modifying the table, adding colors and formatting, but it wasn't enough. Using a slidesgo timeline template, I got this final result: [image: Professional-Learning-Pathways-Process-PRESENTATION-2020-21-1.png] For this next example, a slide with one of the traits of our ISP Educator Framework, I decided to divide the information into two slides. [image: Untitled-presentation-4.png] First, the description of the trait in one slide. A different background to differentiate it from the rest of the slides. [image: Untitled-presentation-5.png] Then the descriptors per category. Bigger text and smaller images for the categories in the center. Changes in the background and color palette. [image: Copy-of-Professional-Learning-Pathways-Process-2020-21-.png] For the following two slides, most of the text was omitted, and both slides were consolidated into only one. [image: Untitled-presentation-9.png] [image: Untitled-presentation-11.png] Here is the result, including links to templates: [image: Untitled-presentation-13.png] I can say that slidesgo was definitely a big ally when revamping slides or creating visuals or infographics from scratch.  And now, let’s design a better future together. Do you have a template?

title: The Cycle of Socialization
body_html:
Have you ever heard or read about the circle of socialization? I recently read about it in a chapter from the fourth edition of Readings for Diversity and Social Justice.  This chapter, The Cycle of socialization, was written by Bobbie Harro and included a graph that I decided to redesign a little to later translate into Spanish to share with family or friends that don’t speak English. We have been learning about the importance of Visual Literacy, infographics, and showing the information in the right way. I updated the graph that summarizes the chapter to make it more appealing: [image: Cycle-of-Socialization-Diagram.png] The chapter on this cycle confirms something that I have been thinking and complaining about a while ago. After reading it, It felt like I had finally found what I needed to support my beliefs. Here is a video recorded using Flipgrid, an online tool to create engaging video discussion experiences around a topic. I had used Flipgrid only once before, but after this experience, I see how I can take advantage of this tool to integrate technology into lessons when planning with my colleagues. In this first video, I mention a word, phrase, and sentence that I found relevant when reading The Cycle of Socialization chapter. This Text Rendering Protocol from National School Reform Faculty (NSRF) is easy to implement and made me more aware of what I was reading as I wanted to pick an interesting word, phrase, and sentence. Scan the QR code to check it out! [image: LuisCarlos_FlipCode-xgmzh5kksrqesozt.png] In this next video, I talk about the word, phrases, and sentences that some of my COETAIL peers picked and connections with the concept of the cycle of socialization. Luiz Mello
  • Word: Unlucky
  • Phase: Virtually invisible.
  • Sentence: Our families or the adults who are raising us. They shape our self-concepts and self-perceptions, the norms and the rules we must follow, the roles we are taught to play, our expectations for the future, and our dreams.
Mooney
  • Word: Humanize
  • Sentence: Our silence is consent. Until our discomfort becomes larger than our comfort, we will probably stay in this cycle.
Mellanie
  • Word: Confusion
  • Phrase: Inherited without our permission 
  • Sentence: We are exposed to roles, rules, and assumptions that are not fair to everyone. 
Cindy
  • Word: Interrupt
  • Phase: We are innocents 
  • Sentence: It should be simple, but it isn’t
[image: LuisCarlos_FlipCode-a23jkmmev6wzbd5x.png] Feel free to add your voice to the conversation on our Community Discussion topic [link removed before import: a Flipgrid grid of responses].

title: Migrating toward Collaboration
body_html:
Our team decided to work on a unit plan for our final project, in this case, revamp one. We started our collaboration through Twitter and then created and shared a Google Doc. Picking a time to meet was not easy because we were all in different time zones (Cambodia, Russia, Belgium, and Panama). Still, we eventually found a time that worked for us (I ended up meeting at 6:00 am Panama time, not a problem for me as I am an early riser). During our first meeting, we went over the sample lesson plans that we had previously shared within our document and decided to go with one of our colleagues’ Migration unit as he was going to teach that unit at his school. Here is the Final Migration Unit Plan [link removed before import: a shared Google Doc]. [image: MIGRATION-UNIT-1.png] When we started reviewing the unit, I learned about the tool used to launch it, the All the World’s Immigration Visualized in 1 Map, a dynamic interactive map showing country-to-country net migration data collected from 2010-2015. I like data, so I found migration not only attractive but relevant and vital, and I love maps, especially the ones showing real-time data or dynamic maps, so I needed to share this fantastic resource here. I immediately started thinking about the many ways to use this tool within the unit. Here you can watch a video of the map. Here the map for you to play around with. One of the significant challenges I had collaborating with my team was that I am not an expert on the subject. I realized that I tend to work with the Science and Math teams because I feel comfortable doing so, but at the same time, I understand how important it is to move out of my comfort zone. I also realized how important it is to ask questions that might seem simple (maybe coming from a place of ignorance on the subject) but need to be considered by the team not to leave out the most basic concepts. Content standards were already in place in the unit planner but were changed or replaced as needed by our colleague. As a team, we decided on what ISTE standards to focus on first by identifying the ones already assessed and then brainstorming to maximize student collaboration or technology tools choice. Because of my background as a Learning Support Specialist and Tech integrationist, I tried to explain how to differentiate the unit and make it more flexible. I wanted students to have options on the tools they could use so that they could pick the right one, but there were limitations on the activities we could do as this unit was going to be carried out by a team, and there were some requirements from the school’s administration as well. For example, infographics were used in the previous units, so that we couldn’t use them. When trying to offer student options by giving them a list of tools that they could use to present their final assessment product (an essay) like Flipgrid and Screencastify, the idea was well-received but eventually left out of the picture. I aimed to hit the ISTE Standards for Students below, but I didn’t manage to do so.
  • Students choose the appropriate platforms and tools for meeting the desired objectives of their creation or communication.
After a brainstorming session on possible activities and the assessment, we picked the following two ISTE Standards:
  • Students communicate complex ideas clearly and effectively by creating or using various digital objects such as visualizations, models, or simulations.
  • Students use collaborative technologies to work with others, including peers, experts, or community members, to examine issues and problems from multiple viewpoints.
As opposed to many collaboration meetings that I am part of, I noticed that I wasn’t even close to being the person running the show, and sometimes we were even kept on task by one of our colleagues. My role in the planning meeting made me feel uncomfortable, and I appreciate that experience. The tool we ultimately chose to carry out the final activity was Parley Ideas. I had never used this tool before. As a result, I had to play around with it and found it easy to use. Knowing that neither the students nor teachers had used the live version of Parlay Ideas, I suggested that we could offer a PD training session for the teaching team. Here is a video of the Parlay Live training session [link removed before import: a meeting recording]. Regarding students getting familiarized with the platform, I suggested that they could have a short (potentially non-academic) practice with a fun question to understand the platform and ensure that the actual activity runs smoothly. As educators, I believe we all learned a little more about our ability to collaborate with diverse teams. The changes made to the lesson due to our collaboration were essential improvements, and students will benefit from them.

title: Make your Frame Work!
body_html:
Using technology in everyday classroom practices usually make educators encounter problems: too many alternatives, not enough time, or lack of a proper framework. In this post, I will tackle frameworks for using educational technology. 

Why frameworks for educational technology?

 A framework provides clarity by offering a structure, a lens for viewing and evaluating technology. It gives direction for planning lessons and implementing technology, and it saves time. These frameworks support teachers to generate classes that will successfully integrate technology and empower students to think critically and creatively.  There are many different types of technology integration frameworks in education, but I will focus on SAMR and TPACK. I will also mention the Framework for 21st Century Learning to connect with the 4Cs.  

What is the SAMR Model? 

This video What Is the SAMR Model? from Common Sense Education explains the model very well.  Dr. Ruben Puentendura created the SAMR model, which works as a framework to help guide the process of incorporating technology into our teaching. SAMR stands for Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition. Most of the time, teachers start at the bottom of the model using technology as a substitution or augmentation within the enhancement block and aim to move to the chart’s top with a more sophisticated use of technology at the modification and redefinition stages within the transformation threshold. This way, the framework guides teachers to ideate, plan, and create learning experiences that effectively and meaningfully use technology. [caption id="attachment_399" align="aligncenter" width="1200"][image: samr_r2.png] Image Modified by Schoology from Original by Lefflerd’s on Wikimedia Commons[/caption] It is not always necessary to include technology in our lessons, and redefining the learning experiences shouldn’t be the goal all the time. To avoid this, we can ask ourselves these reflection questions mentioned in the video above: 
  • What will I gain from replacing old technologies with new technologies?
  • Have I added an enhancement to the task process that can not be accomplished whit the older technology at a fundamental level?
  • Does this modification depend upon the new technology?
  • How is the new task made possible by the latest technology? 

Framework for 21st Century Learning

In the “Framework for 21st Century Learning” document, we can read that it “was developed with input from educators, education experts, and business leaders to define and illustrate the skills, knowledge, expertise, and support systems that students need to succeed in work, life, and citizenship.”  You can learn more about it by watching this video: 21st Century Learning & Life Skills: Framework. [image: rainbow-01304bcd241d306876be2bff000011dea3.png] As you can acknowledge from the image above, the framework’s outer arc contains three different groups: Life & Career Skills, Learning & Innovation Skills, and Information, Media, & Technology Skills that add up to 12 skills.  At the top, we have the Learning & Innovation Skills, which include:
  • Creativity and Innovation
  • Critical Thinking and Problem Solving
  • Communication
  • Collaboration
These skills, commonly known as the 4Cs, prepare students for today’s complicated life and work environments. 

4Cs

In the video “What are the 4Cs?” you can learn how critical these skills are and how digital tools can foster them in today’s students. This set of skills connects back to the SAMR model as it is on its last stage that technology redefines the task to include the 4Cs, as shown below. [image: 4CS-1.png]

TPACK Model

 According to Matt Koehler in TPACK Explained  – TPACK.ORG, “Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) attempts to identify the nature of knowledge required by teachers for technology integration in their teaching while addressing the complex, multifaceted and situated nature of teacher knowledge.” Watch the “What is the TPACK Model?” video for an introduction to this framework. [caption id="attachment_401" align="aligncenter" width="768"][image: TPACK-new-768x768-1.png] TPACK diagram reproduced by permission of the publisher, ©2012 by tpack.org.[/caption] In the diagram, the overlapping circles define the seven components of TPACK, seven types of knowledge:
  • Technological Knowledge (TK)
  • Content Knowledge (CK)
  • Pedagogical Knowledge (PK)
  • Technological Content Knowledge (TCK)
  • Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK)
  • Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK)
  • Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPCK)
The principle is that we should not teach Technology, Pedagogy, and Content Knowledge in isolation, but they should merge in our lessons. Our goal is to position ourselves in the center of the diagram, where all types of knowledge combine.  When using this diagram as a reference, we can ask ourselves questions such as:
  • What are the areas you feel the strongest?
  • Which areas could you use improvements to help enhance students learning?

How can we blend TPACK and SAMR?

I found “The Blended Ladder” created by Dr. RJ Gravel, Dr. Josh Mika, and Ms. Shannon Soger to be the best way of visualizing, understanding, and blending SAMR and TPACK. Reflections

After exposure to all these frameworks, I understand how these structures are interconnected. Besides that, I realize an excellent area for growth at my current school regarding tech integration. We haven’t established what model or combination of models we want to use when creating learning experiences. As a tech coach and integrationist, I will keep this in mind when collaborating with my colleagues and making it my goal to create awareness of these models and even publicize them with posters when we are back on campus and virtually while we remain online.
